H1.text: Every equation you have solved so far had an answer you could point to on the number line.

H2.text: x minus three equals zero? Point at three. x squared equals four? Point at two, or minus two.

H3.text: Last night, Aarav met one that broke the rule. A new chapter begins with it.

H4.text: x squared plus one equals zero. He tried every number he could think of. Not one worked.

H5.text: Is the equation broken, or is the number line too small?

P1.text: So why does no number work?

P2.text: Three squared is nine. Minus three squared is also nine, because minus times minus is plus.

P3.text: Zero squared is zero. So a square is never negative.

P4.text: Watch x slide along the line. x squared never drops below zero.

P5.text: So x squared plus one is always at least one. It can never reach zero.

L1.text: Now draw the graph of y equals x squared plus c, and let c change.

L2.text: Where the curve crosses the x axis, y is zero. Those points are the real solutions.

L3.text: At c equal to minus four, the curve cuts the axis at two and at minus two.

L4.text: Let c count up. The crossings move in, to one and minus one.

L5.text: At c equal to zero, the curve just touches the axis.

L6.text: Past zero, it lifts off. No crossing, so no real solution.

L7.text: At c equal to one, our equation, it floats one full unit above the axis.

D1.text: Now prove it in four small steps.

D2.text: Step one. Start with x squared plus one equals zero.

D3.text: Step two. Subtract one from both sides. x squared equals minus one.

D4.text: Step three. But every real square is zero or more.

D5.text: Step four. Nothing is zero or more and also minus one. So no real number solves it.

S1.text: Side by side. x squared minus one equals zero crosses the axis twice.

S2.text: x squared plus one equals zero never crosses. No real solution.

S3.text: Now you try. Does x squared plus four equals zero have a real solution? Pause and decide.

S4.text: No! x squared is never negative, so x squared plus four is at least four.

Z1.text: Numbers have run out like this before.

Z2.text: x plus five equals two needs a negative number. Two x equals three needs a fraction.

Z3.text: x squared equals two needs root two. Each time, the number system grew.

Z4.text: Now x squared equals minus one is stuck again.

Z5.text: The Indian mathematicians Mahavira and Bhaskara wrote that a negative number has no square root.

Z6.text: In fifteen forty five, Cardan solved a puzzle and got five plus root minus fifteen. He called such answers useless.

I1.text: So mathematicians grew the number system once more.

I2.text: They named a new number, i, whose square is minus one. In symbols, i is the square root of minus one.

I3.text: Now x equals i works. i squared plus one is minus one plus one, which is zero.

T1.text: Remember this. No real number has a negative square. That is why we need a new kind of number.

U1.text: But where does i live? Not on the number line.

U2.text: Multiplying by minus one turns three into minus three. That is a half turn.

U3.text: i times i is minus one. So multiplying by i twice makes a half turn.

U4.text: Then multiplying by i once is a quarter turn. Off the line, straight up.

U5.text: So complex numbers need a second direction.

U6.text: Quick one. Start at three and multiply by i twice. Where do you land? Pause and think.

U7.text: Minus three! Two quarter turns make one half turn.

W2.text: Show that x squared plus four x plus five equals zero has no real solution. Then solve it with i.

W3.text: Step one. Write five as four plus one.

W4.text: Step two. That gives x plus two, squared, equals minus one.

W5.text: Step three. A real square cannot be negative. So there is no real solution.

W6.text: Step four. With i, x plus two is i or minus i. So x is minus two plus or minus i.

W7.text: The graph agrees. Its lowest point is at height one, so it never touches the axis.

X2.text: Many students say minus one solves x squared equals minus one.

X3.text: But minus one, in brackets, squared, is minus one times minus one. That is plus one, so it is not a solution.

J1.text: Where is this asked? In PUC board exams. Show that an equation has no real solution, then solve it with i.

Q1.text: Exam level now. For how many integers c is there no real solution? Pause and solve.

A2.text: Complete the square. x minus two, squared, equals four minus c.

A3.text: A real square is never negative. So there is no real solution exactly when c is more than four.

A4.text: At c equal to four, x equals two still works. So c is five to twenty: sixteen integers.

Y1.text: Can you answer these three questions without help?

Y2.text: One. Why does x squared plus nine equals zero have no real solution?

Y3.text: Two. For which values of c does y equals x squared plus c miss the x axis?

Y4.text: Three. Is minus one, in brackets, squared, equal to minus one?
